content: The treatment of vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC), caused primarily by Candida albicans, has been extensively studied through systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The studies included women, adolescents, and pregnant individuals diagnosed with C. albicans. The interventions compared oral fluconazole (150 mg single dose) with various intravaginal antifungal agents, including clotrimazole, econazole, fenticonazole, itraconazole, miconazole, and nystatin, delivered in different doses and formulations. Key Findings: 1. Clinical and Microbiological Cure Rates: Oral fluconazole (150 mg single dose) was found to have similar short-term and long-term clinical and microbiological cure rates compared to intravaginal clotrimazole (200 mg for 3 days) and other azole antifungals. A Cochrane review reported that single-dose clotrimazole showed little to no difference in cure rates compared to fluconazole or longer durations of clotrimazole treatment. 2. Pregnant Women: In pregnant women, imidazoles (e.g., clotrimazole) demonstrated higher cure rates (84%) compared to nystatin (53%) in four RCTs. Clotrimazole administered as vaginal tablets or cream for 6–7 days was more effective than single-dose treatments. 3. Recurrent Vulvovaginal Candidiasis: For recurrent VVC, one RCT compared oral fluconazole with vaginal nystatin suppositories (200,000 units daily for 14 days). Fluconazole showed higher cure rates (78%) compared to nystatin. 4. Treatment Preferences: Twelve trials involving 2,206 participants assessed patient preferences for oral versus intravaginal antifungal treatments. Between 52% and 93% of participants preferred oral treatment, although selective reporting was noted in some studies. 5. Side Effects: Side effects were generally mild and comparable between oral and intravaginal treatments. Fluconazole and clotrimazole were well-tolerated, with no significant differences in adverse events. 6. Comparisons with Other Antifungals: Fluconazole was compared with miconazole, econazole, and fenticonazole in various formulations. The results showed no significant differences in cure rates, although some studies had limited sample sizes or methodological differences. 7. HIV-Infected Women: A Cochrane review evaluated interventions for VVC in women with HIV. Fluconazole and other azoles were effective, but the evidence was limited by the small number of studies. Evidence Synthesis: The evidence was synthesized using the GRADE approach, and summary findings were presented in tables. The systematic reviews and meta-analyses informed the World Health Organization (WHO) treatment recommendations for Candida albicans and other sexually transmitted infections, including Trichomonas vaginalis, Mycoplasma genitalium, bacterial vaginosis, and human papillomavirus (HPV). Search Strategy: The search for systematic reviews was conducted in Epistemonikos up to August 2023, identifying seven high-quality reviews. Primary studies were searched in databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and LILACS, covering the period from 1996 to May 2022. No new RCTs were identified in the updated search. Conclusion: Oral fluconazole (150 mg single dose) is an effective and well-tolerated treatment for uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis, with comparable efficacy to intravaginal azoles. In pregnant women, imidazoles like clotrimazole are preferred over nystatin due to higher cure rates. Patient preference often favors oral treatment, but both oral and intravaginal options remain viable depending on individual circumstances and clinical judgment.
